warmup.q: A settlement batch takes 1,025 ms on one worker. 25 ms of that is serial: the coordinator starts the job and commits the result, and nothing else can run meanwhile. The other 1,000 ms split perfectly across workers. How long does the batch take on 1,000 workers?
warmup.why: The 1,000 ms of parallel work becomes 1 ms, but the 25 ms of serial work doesn't shrink at all: 26 ms in total, a speed-up of about 39 against a ceiling of 1,025 / 25 = 41. That ceiling is Amdahl's law. "About 1 ms" divides everything by 1,000. A job can get slower with more workers, as the lab shows, but only when the workers also have to coordinate with each other, which this question rules out.

sections.h: Scaling up: one bigger machine, until it stops paying
sections.html:
The nightly settlement batch adds up a day of payments per merchant. It takes 40 minutes and the business wants 10. The simplest thing to try is a machine with four times the cores. That is scaling up, or vertical scaling. All the threads share one machine's memory, so this is also called a shared-memory architecture, and coordinating them is cheap: a lock in memory, a shared hash map.

The ceiling is higher than most people expect. In December 2024 AWS made the u7inh-32tb.480xlarge instance available: 1,920 vCPUs and 32 TiB of memory in one 16-socket server, with 200 Gbit/s of network.

Two things stop you anyway. First, price grows faster than size: the largest machines cost more per core than ordinary ones. Second, four times the cores rarely do four times the work, because part of the work can't be split. Say 2.5% of the batch is serial: a coordinator reads the list of input files before anyone starts and commits the result at the end. Gene Amdahl's 1967 argument gives the limit. With a serial share σ, N workers give a speed-up of at most 1 / (σ + (1 − σ) / N). At σ = 2.5%, 40 workers give about 20 times, and no number of workers gives more than 1 / 0.025 = 40.

Amdahl assumed that the rest splits perfectly. Real workers also have to keep in step. Cache lines bounce between cores, a released lock wakes every thread waiting for it, a shuffle makes every worker send data to every other worker. That cost grows with the number of pairs of workers, N(N − 1), so past some point another worker makes the whole job slower. Neil Gunther's Universal Scalability Law (USL) adds that term to Amdahl's:

C(N) = N / (1 + α(N − 1) + βN(N − 1))

C(N) is the throughput of N workers relative to one. α is contention: the share of time spent waiting for something only one worker can use at a time. β is coherency: the cost of every pair of workers keeping in agreement. With β = 0 this is Amdahl's law. With β > 0 the curve peaks at N = √((1 − α) / β) and then falls.

Keep those two letters for the whole lesson. Every architecture below is defined by what its workers share, and what they share is where they wait (α) and what they have to keep in agreement (β).

The lab measures a simulated settlement batch on 1 to 128 workers and fits the USL to the throughput. It finds α ≈ 0.03 and β ≈ 0.0005, a predicted peak at 45 workers, and the measured best is 48. The same law fits threads on one machine and machines in a cluster; only the shared thing changes.

figure.caption: The lab's settlement batch. Amdahl's curve (dashed) only knows the serial share and keeps climbing; the USL fit (blue) also charges for every pair of workers and turns down where the measurements do.

try.title: Find the peak, then remove the shuffle
steps: From the labs folder, run the demo below. It runs the settlement batch on 1 to 128 simulated workers in virtual time, checks every run against one thread's answer, and fits the USL.
Before it prints, predict: does 128 workers beat 64?
Run it again with -Pargs='0 20', which makes the shuffle's cost per pair of workers zero. What happens to β and to the curve?
Now try -Pargs='2 20': a shuffle four times as expensive per pair. Where does the peak move?

code.title: ScalingDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.found.l05.demo import kotlin.random.Random // A copy of the lab's Settlement.kt (demos can't see src/main), plus a main that measures it. // // The system under test: the nightly settlement batch, which adds up one day of payments per merchant. // It runs either on one thread with a hash map, or on a simulated cluster of N workers. Time is // virtual: the code really does the work (the totals are real), and every step adds its cost, in // nanoseconds, to a clock. So every run gives the same numbers on every laptop. /** One day of payments: `merchant[i]` was paid `amountCents[i]`. A few big merchants get most payments. */ class Payments(val merchant: IntArray, val amountCents: LongArray) { val size: Int get() = merchant.size } fun paymentsOfTheDay(count: Int = 1_000_000, merchants: Int = 5_000, seed: Long = 1): Payments { val random = Random(seed) val m = IntArray(count) { (merchants * random.nextDouble().let { it * it * it }).toInt() } // skewed to low ids val a = LongArray(count) { 100L + random.nextLong(50_000) } return Payments(m, a) } /** What each step costs in virtual time. The defaults are made up but keep real proportions. */ data class Costs( /** One thread, a plain loop over an array and a hash map. */ val singlePaymentNs: Double = 100.0, /** Serial: the coordinator schedules the job and starts the workers. Nothing else can run meanwhile. */ val startupMs: Double = 20.0, /** On a worker: decode one row through the framework and add it to a partial sum. */ val clusterPaymentNs: Double = 1_000.0, /** The shuffle: every worker opens a connection to every other worker and waits for its answer. */ val perPeerMs: Double = 0.5, /** Sending one partial sum (merchant, amount) to the worker that owns that merchant, and merging it. */ val perEntryNs: Double = 500.0, /** Serial: the coordinator collects the results and commits them. */ val commitMs: Double = 5.0, ) /** How long a run took, in virtual seconds, and the total per merchant it computed. */ class BatchRun(val seconds: Double, val totals: Map<Int, Long>) fun runOnOneThread(p: Payments, costs: Costs = Costs()): BatchRun { val totals = HashMap<Int, Long>() for (i in 0 until p.size) totals.merge(p.merchant[i], p.amountCents[i], Long::plus) return BatchRun(p.size * costs.singlePaymentNs / 1e9, totals) } /** * Runs the batch on [workers] simulated machines that share nothing: each reads its own slice of the * input, sums it per merchant, then sends each partial sum to the worker that owns the merchant * (`merchant % workers`). Phases end with a barrier, so each phase lasts as long as its slowest worker. */ fun runOnCluster(p: Payments, workers: Int, costs: Costs = Costs()): BatchRun { require(workers >= 1) var ns = costs.startupMs * 1e6 // serial // map: each worker sums its slice of the input val partial = Array(workers) { HashMap<Int, Long>() } var slowestMap = 0.0 for (w in 0 until workers) { val from = (p.size.toLong() * w / workers).toInt() val to = (p.size.toLong() * (w + 1) / workers).toInt() for (i in from until to) partial[w].merge(p.merchant[i], p.amountCents[i], Long::plus) slowestMap = maxOf(slowestMap, (to - from) * costs.clusterPaymentNs) } ns += slowestMap // shuffle: partial sums travel to their owners; every pair of workers pays a connection val received = LongArray(workers) val sent = LongArray(workers) val totals = HashMap<Int, Long>() for (w in 0 until workers) for ((merchant, sum) in partial[w]) { val owner = merchant % workers if (owner != w) { sent[w]++; received[owner]++ } totals.merge(merchant, sum, Long::plus) } var slowestShuffle = 0.0 for (w in 0 until workers) { val t = (workers - 1) * costs.perPeerMs * 1e6 + (sent[w] + received[w]) * costs.perEntryNs slowestShuffle = maxOf(slowestShuffle, t) } ns += slowestShuffle ns += costs.commitMs * 1e6 // serial return BatchRun(ns / 1e9, totals) } // Run from the labs folder: // ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.found.l05.demo.ScalingDemoKt --console=plain -q // ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.found.l05.demo.ScalingDemoKt --console=plain -q -Pargs='0.5 20' // The arguments are the shuffle's cost per pair of workers (ms) and the job's startup time (ms). fun main(args: Array<String>) { val costs = Costs( perPeerMs = args.getOrNull(0)?.toDouble() ?: Costs().perPeerMs, startupMs = args.getOrNull(1)?.toDouble() ?: Costs().startupMs, ) val payments = paymentsOfTheDay() val one = runOnOneThread(payments, costs) println("settlement of %,d payments, %,d merchants".format(payments.size, one.totals.size)) println("one thread, plain loop: %.1f ms".format(one.seconds * 1000)) println() println("workers time (ms) payments/s speed-up") val measured = linkedMapOf<Int, Double>() val counts = listOf(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128) for (n in counts) { val run = runOnCluster(payments, n, costs) check(run.totals == one.totals) { "the cluster got a different answer" } measured[n] = payments.size / run.seconds println("%7d %11.1f %,12.0f %10.1f".format(n, run.seconds * 1000, measured[n], measured[n]!! / measured[1]!!)) } val fit = fitUsl(measured) println() println("USL fit: alpha %.4f beta %.6f peak at %.0f workers".format(fit.alpha, fit.beta, uslPeak(fit.alpha, fit.beta))) val best = measured.maxBy { it.value } println("measured best: %d workers, %.1f ms".format(best.key, payments.size / best.value * 1000)) // COST: walk up from 1 worker. Time falls, bottoms out, then rises, so once it rises the search can stop. var previous = Double.MAX_VALUE for (n in 1..4096) { val t = runOnCluster(payments, n, costs).seconds if (t < one.seconds) { println("COST: $n workers to beat one thread (%.1f ms)".format(t * 1000)); return } if (t > previous) { println("COST: unbounded, no number of workers beats one thread"); return } previous = t } } fun usl(n: Int, alpha: Double, beta: Double) = n / (1.0 + alpha * (n - 1) + beta * n * (n - 1.0)) fun uslPeak(alpha: Double, beta: Double) = if (beta <= 0) Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY else kotlin.math.sqrt((1 - alpha) / beta) class Fit(val alpha: Double, val beta: Double) fun fitUsl(m: Map<Int, Double>): Fit { val x1 = m.getValue(1) val pts = m.filterKeys { it > 1 }.map { (n, x) -> (n - 1.0) to (n / (x / x1) - 1.0) / (n - 1.0) } val mx = pts.map { it.first }.average() val mz = pts.map { it.second }.average() val slope = pts.sumOf { (x, z) -> (x - mx) * (z - mz) } / pts.sumOf { (x, _) -> (x - mx) * (x - mx) } return Fit(alpha = mz - slope * mx - slope, beta = slope) }

sections.h: Three ways to share: memory, disk or nothing
sections.html:
When one machine isn't enough, you add machines, and the question becomes what they share.

Shared memory is the single machine from the last section. Coordination is cheap, but it is one machine: one power supply, one motherboard, one place where a single fault takes everything down: a single point of failure, in lesson 3's terms.

Shared disk means several machines, each with its own CPUs and memory, all reading and writing the same disks over a fast storage network, a SAN (storage area network) or a NAS (network-attached storage). Oracle RAC is the example you may run at work. Several database instances open the same data files, so any instance can serve any query. Two instances must not change the same block at the same moment, so RAC keeps a global lock manager. When instance 2 needs a block that instance 1 has changed, a mechanism called Cache Fusion ships the block from instance 1's memory over a private interconnect. That lock and block traffic is shared disk's β, and it is why shared-disk clusters have stayed small: a handful of nodes, mostly for availability and for on-premises data warehouses.

Shared nothing means each node has its own CPUs, memory and disks, and nodes cooperate only by sending messages over an ordinary network. The data is split into partitions and each node owns some of them, which the Partitioning track builds properly. Nodes can be cheap ordinary machines, the cluster can grow one node at a time, and it can span racks, availability zones and regions, so it survives losing one of them. Kafka brokers, Cassandra and CockroachDB work this way. So does your PostgreSQL primary with a streaming standby: the standby keeps its own copy on its own disk. The price is twofold. Something must decide where every piece of data lives and route requests to it. And every interaction between nodes is a network message that can be lost, delayed or duplicated, which the Faults, time and truth track takes apart.

The lab's batch is shared-nothing. Each worker sums its own slice of the payments, then the workers swap partial sums so that each one ends up owning some merchants' totals. Its α is the coordinator's startup and commit. Its β is the shuffle, in which every worker opens a connection to every other.

Most real systems mix the three. Each Kafka broker is a shared-memory machine inside a shared-nothing cluster. And the cloud brought shared disk back in a new form, which the next section opens up.

try.title: Classify what you run
steps: For each system, say which architecture it uses and name the one thing its nodes or threads wait for: Oracle RAC; a single PostgreSQL server; a PostgreSQL primary with a streaming standby; a three-broker Kafka cluster; a Redis Cluster with six nodes.
Then pick one you use at work and say what happens to it when one machine dies.
try.expect: Oracle RAC is shared disk: instances wait for the global lock manager and for blocks shipped by Cache Fusion. A single PostgreSQL server is shared memory: backends wait for locks and buffers in its shared memory, and the machine is a single point of failure. A primary with a standby is shared nothing: the standby has its own copy and waits for WAL (the database's change log) sent over the network. Kafka and Redis Cluster are shared nothing too: each partition, or each range of keys, lives on its own nodes, and clients must find the right node. If a Kafka broker dies, another broker that holds a copy of each of its partitions takes over; if the single PostgreSQL machine dies, everything waits until it is back.

sections.h: Separating storage from compute: shared disk, rebuilt for the cloud
sections.html:
A cloud instance's local disk disappears with the instance: when it fails, or when you move to a bigger size on a different physical machine. Network block storage such as Amazon EBS survives, but it is a separate service, so every disk I/O becomes a network call. Run a classic database on it and mirror it to a second zone, and each transaction turns into many network writes: data pages, log, more copies.

Amazon measured exactly that in the 2017 Aurora paper. In a 30-minute write-only benchmark on the same instance type, MySQL mirrored across zones completed 780,000 transactions at 7.4 I/Os each. Aurora completed 27,378,000 at 0.95 I/Os each: 35 times the transactions, with 7.7 times fewer I/Os per transaction, while keeping six copies of the data.

Aurora's trick is that the log is the database. The database instance sends only redo log records, the short descriptions of what each change did, to a separate storage fleet, and the storage nodes apply them to pages themselves. The volume is cut into 10 GB segments. Each segment has six copies, two in each of three availability zones; a write counts once four copies have it, and a read needs three. The stepper shows what that buys.

Other systems split storage from compute the same way, each with its own storage service:

  • Snowflake (2016) keeps table files in S3. Compute runs in "virtual warehouses", groups of EC2 workers that cache the files they read on local SSD. Several warehouses can query the same data at once without slowing each other, and resizing a warehouse moves no data.
  • Neon runs stateless PostgreSQL compute. The WAL goes to safekeepers, which agree on it with the Paxos protocol: a commit counts once a quorum has it. A pageserver rebuilds pages from the WAL, object storage keeps the history, and compute can shut down to zero when idle.
  • Kafka 3.9 (November 2024) made tiered storage production-ready: old log segments move to object storage. KIP-1150, "Diskless Topics", has since been accepted as a design. Such topics keep their data in object storage and use broker disks only as a cache. The motivation is money: AWS charges $0.02 per GiB that crosses availability zones, and classic replication sends every byte across zones. The price is higher produce latency, chosen per topic.
  • S3 Express One Zone offers single-digit-millisecond object storage in one zone. In April 2025 its storage price in us-east-1 fell from $0.16 to $0.11 per GB-month.

So when you meet any of these products, ask one question first: where is the durable copy, and what is only a cache?

System Durable copy Only a cache
Aurora 6 copies of each 10 GB segment, across 3 zones the instance's buffer pool
Snowflake files in S3 each warehouse's local SSD
Neon WAL on safekeepers, then object storage compute memory and local NVMe
Kafka diskless topic object storage broker disks

frames.say: The storage fleet copies the segment from a surviving copy onto a new node. A 10 GB segment takes about 10 seconds on a 10 Gbit/s link, so the window in which one more failure could hurt is seconds long. With four copies again, writes resume. This is why Aurora cuts a volume into small segments: repair time, not the failure rate, is the number it can shrink.

try.title: Check Aurora's quorums by brute force
steps: Run the demo below. It tries every possible set of lost copies (0 to 6 of them) and counts the cases where writes (4 healthy copies) and reads (3) still work.
Predict first: out of the 20 ways to lose three copies, how many still allow writes? How many allow reads?
Change WRITE_QUORUM to 3 and run it again. Writes now survive one more lost copy. Look at the two overlap checks at the end: what could go wrong?

code.title: QuorumDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.found.l05.demo // Aurora's storage layout, checked by brute force: 6 copies of each 10 GB segment, 2 in each of // 3 availability zones. A write needs 4 copies to acknowledge it, a read needs 3. // Run from the labs folder: // ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.found.l05.demo.QuorumDemoKt --console=plain -q val COPIES = listOf("a1", "a2", "b1", "b2", "c1", "c2") // the letter is the availability zone const val WRITE_QUORUM = 4 const val READ_QUORUM = 3 fun main() { println("every way to lose copies, and what still works (write needs $WRITE_QUORUM, read needs $READ_QUORUM)") println("lost cases writes ok reads ok") for (lost in 0..COPIES.size) { val cases = subsets(COPIES, lost) val writes = cases.count { COPIES.size - it.size >= WRITE_QUORUM } val reads = cases.count { COPIES.size - it.size >= READ_QUORUM } println("%4d %6d %10d %9d".format(lost, cases.size, writes, reads)) } println() for ((name, down) in listOf( "zone a fails" to setOf("a1", "a2"), "zone a fails, then c2 dies" to setOf("a1", "a2", "c2"), "zones a and b fail" to setOf("a1", "a2", "b1", "b2"), )) { val alive = COPIES.size - down.size println("%-28s alive %d writes %-4s reads %s".format( name, alive, if (alive >= WRITE_QUORUM) "yes" else "no", if (alive >= READ_QUORUM) "yes" else "no")) } println() // why these numbers: any read set must meet the last write set, and two writes can't both win val overlapRW = subsets(COPIES, WRITE_QUORUM).all { w -> subsets(COPIES, READ_QUORUM).all { r -> w.any(r::contains) } } val overlapWW = subsets(COPIES, WRITE_QUORUM).all { w1 -> subsets(COPIES, WRITE_QUORUM).all { w2 -> w1.any(w2::contains) } } val n = COPIES.size println("every read quorum overlaps every write quorum: $overlapRW ($WRITE_QUORUM + $READ_QUORUM > $n is ${WRITE_QUORUM + READ_QUORUM > n})") println("every two write quorums overlap: $overlapWW ($WRITE_QUORUM + $WRITE_QUORUM > $n is ${2 * WRITE_QUORUM > n})") val repairSeconds = 10.0 * 8 / 10 // 10 GB is 80 gigabits; at 10 Gbit/s println("re-copying one 10 GB segment at 10 Gbit/s: %.0f s, before network and disk overheads".format(repairSeconds)) } fun subsets(items: List<String>, k: Int): List<Set<String>> = if (k == 0) listOf(emptySet()) else if (items.size < k) emptyList() else subsets(items.drop(1), k - 1).map { it + items[0] } + subsets(items.drop(1), k)

try.expect:
Output trimmed (the rows for 5 and 6 lost copies are all zeros):

lost  cases  writes ok  reads ok
   0      1          1         1
   1      6          6         6
   2     15         15        15
   3     20          0        20
   4     15          0         0

zone a fails                 alive 4  writes yes  reads yes
zone a fails, then c2 dies   alive 3  writes no   reads yes
zones a and b fail           alive 2  writes no   reads no

every read quorum overlaps every write quorum: true   (4 + 3 > 6 is true)
every two write quorums overlap:               true   (4 + 4 > 6 is true)

Any two losses, a whole zone included, leave writes working; any three leave reads working. With a write quorum of 3, the three-loss row says 20 20 and both checks print false. Two writes can each be acknowledged by three different copies (3 + 3 is not more than 6), so two conflicting writes could both "succeed", and a read of three copies could miss the latest write entirely. The Replication track builds quorums properly.

sections.h: Serverless and microservices: elastic and independent, at a price
sections.html:
Two more ways to grow past one machine are mostly about money and people rather than data.

Serverless, or functions as a service, brings metered billing to running code, the way cloud storage did to disks. You don't pick machines. The provider starts copies of your function as requests arrive and bills for the time they run. The costs are limits on how long a function may run, restricted runtimes, and cold starts: the first request to a new copy waits while the runtime starts and your code initializes. On AWS Lambda, since 1 August 2025 that initialization (the INIT phase) is billed for on-demand functions too. AWS says cold starts happen in under 1% of invocations, and for Java its SnapStart feature restores a snapshot taken after initialization instead of initializing again. "Serverless" has also become a label for any autoscaled, usage-billed service, such as BigQuery or various managed Kafka offerings. The functions still run on servers; you just don't manage them.

Serverless suits spiky, light work. Steady heavy work can cost far more. In 2023 the Prime Video team described its audio and video quality-monitoring service, built from AWS Step Functions steps that passed video frames through S3. Moving it into a single process on EC2 and ECS cut its infrastructure cost by over 90%. Commentators pointed out that this was one service and that the savings came mostly from per-step orchestration and S3 charges, not from monoliths in general.

Microservices split one application into services that each own one job, one API and one database, each run by one team. Each service can be deployed on its own schedule and given its own hardware, and its team can change the implementation behind the API. Sharing a database between services is avoided, because then the schema becomes part of every service's API. The costs: testing one service needs the others running; every service needs deployment, scaling, logs, metrics and an on-call rotation (which is why Kubernetes became common); changing an API breaks callers, often late, in staging or production; and keeping data consistent across services becomes the application's problem, because transactions don't span services' databases. The Encoding track covers evolving APIs, and the Transactions track covers commits across machines.

Microservices are mostly an answer to an organizational problem: letting many teams move without waiting for each other. For a payments platform with twelve teams that is worth a lot. For three teams it is usually overhead. They are not, by themselves, how a system scales: the scaling principle is independence, and partitioning one database gives you that too.

sections.h: When one machine is enough: the COST of a cluster
sections.html:
A speed-up curve compares a system with itself. It never says whether you needed the system at all. In 2015 Frank McSherry, Michael Isard and Derek Murray proposed a metric that does: COST, the Configuration that Outperforms a Single Thread. It is the hardware a system needs before it beats a competent single-threaded program on the same problem.

They took graph-processing results published at top systems conferences and ran the same problems with one thread on a 2014 laptop. On the twitter_rv graph (41.7 million nodes, 1.47 billion edges), 20 iterations of PageRank took 857 s on Spark with 128 cores, 419 s on GraphX with 128 cores, and 300 s on one thread reading from SSD. Laying the edges out in a better order (a Hilbert curve) and reading from RAM brought one thread down to 110 s. For finding connected components, the label-propagation algorithm that suits these frameworks took 1,784 s on Spark and 251 s on GraphX, both with 128 cores. One thread running union-find, an older algorithm that does far less work but doesn't parallelize as neatly, took 15 s. By their reading, GraphLab needed 512 cores to beat one thread at PageRank, and GraphX never did: its COST is unbounded.

Why so bad? Frameworks pay per record: generic rows, serialization, network buffers, scheduling. They pay per round, too, in coordination. And they push you toward algorithms that parallelize well rather than algorithms that do little work. A system that adds parallelizable overhead even looks better on a speed-up curve, because one worker is so slow.

The lab measures the same thing on its settlement batch. A plain loop with a hash map adds up a million payments in 100 ms. The simulated cluster pays ten times as much per payment, plus startup and a shuffle. It needs 16 workers just to match one thread, and its best is 73.7 ms at 48 workers. Make the shuffle cost 2 ms per pair of workers and no cluster size ever wins.

Remember the size of one machine today: 1,920 vCPUs and 32 TiB of memory. Single-node engines such as DuckDB and SQLite handle data sets that needed clusters ten years ago. Jordan Tigani, who worked on BigQuery, estimated in 2023 that most of its customers stored under a terabyte in total. There are still good reasons to distribute: data that outgrows a machine, ingest of several terabytes a day, surviving the loss of a zone, users on several continents. Measure your COST before you assume you have one of them. The Batch processing track returns to this question with real engines.

try.title: Find the COST, then break it
steps: Look at the last line of the demo output from the first Try it: the COST of the default cluster.
Run the demo with -Pargs='0.5 200': the same shuffle, but a job startup of 200 ms instead of 20 ms, which is still short for a real cluster framework. Predict the COST before you run it.
Which of the cluster's costs would you attack first to make it win, and what would that do to the USL's α and β?
try.expect:
Default costs: COST: 16 workers to beat one thread (99.7 ms), against 100.0 ms for one thread.

With a 200 ms startup:

USL fit: alpha 0.1744  beta 0.000402  peak at 45 workers
measured best: 48 workers, 253.7 ms
COST: unbounded, no number of workers beats one thread

The startup is serial, so it raises α (from 0.029 to 0.174) and puts a floor of 200 ms under every run: no number of workers gets below the 100 ms of one thread. Cutting serial work lowers α; cutting per-record overhead shrinks the whole cluster curve, which is what lowers the COST most.

refs.title: McSherry, Isard and Murray, Scalability! But at what COST? (HotOS 2015)
Jordan Tigani, Big Data is Dead (MotherDuck)

analogy: Shared memory is one kitchen with more cooks: they share the fridge and the stove, which is easy until they queue for the one oven. Shared disk is several kitchens sharing one pantry down the hall: each has its own stove, but two cooks can't take the last bag of flour, so someone has to hand out pantry keys. Shared nothing is a chain of restaurants, each with its own pantry and its own copy of the recipes, which coordinate by phone. Separating storage from compute is a central warehouse that delivers to kitchens that keep only today's ingredients. The analogy breaks at the phone calls. Restaurants rarely need to agree on anything within milliseconds, while database nodes do it on every write, and a phone call that never connects can't leave a restaurant unsure whether its order was placed. A lost network message can leave a node exactly that unsure.
world: Your Oracle database may well be RAC: shared disk, where a hot block that every instance updates (a sequence, a merchant balance) becomes Cache Fusion traffic between nodes, the β of this lesson. Your Kafka cluster is shared nothing: each partition is replicated to brokers in other zones, and if those zones are on AWS, every replicated byte pays cross-zone transfer, which is exactly the bill KIP-1150's diskless topics were written to cut. Before you move the settlement batch to Spark, measure its COST: run it with one thread over the day's payments in memory (a few million rows fit easily) and see whether the cluster beats that. And when a team proposes splitting the payments service into five microservices, ask which teams that frees from waiting for each other, because that, and not throughput, is what you buy.
mistake: Adding workers without measuring the curve. A slow job gets more threads, more pods or a bigger connection pool, and gets slower, because the work waits on one shared thing: a lock on a hot ledger row, a sequence, one database's CPU, a shuffle in which everybody talks to everybody. People expect parallelism to be free because each extra worker looks independent. The fix is to measure throughput at four or five worker counts, fit the USL, and read α and β. A big α means find the serial step and shrink it. A big β means find what every worker keeps in agreement and stop sharing it. Only then add workers, and stop well before the peak.

a.label: one thread
a.title: runOnOneThread: 1,000,000 payments in 100 ms
a.html: val totals = HashMap<Int, Long>() for (i in 0 until p.size) { totals.merge(p.merchant[i], p.amountCents[i], Long::plus) } // cost: 100 ns per payment, nothing else

b.label: simulated cluster
b.title: runOnCluster: phases, each as slow as its slowest worker
b.html:
startup        20 ms              serial (alpha)
map            1,000 ns x payments / N
shuffle        0.5 ms x (N - 1)   every pair connects (beta)
               + 500 ns per partial sum sent or received
commit         5 ms               serial (alpha)

N = 16: 99.7 ms   N = 48: 73.7 ms   N = 128: 99.4 ms

compare.note: Both compute exactly the same totals; the lab checks that. The loop on the left has no startup, no shuffle and no per-record framework cost, so the cluster needs 16 workers just to catch up with it. The cluster's own costs map onto the USL: startup and commit are the serial share α, and the per-pair shuffle is the coherency term β that makes 128 workers slower than 48.

worked.title: Fit the USL to four measurements by hand

steps.say: Take four throughput measurements from the demo and compute the relative capacity C = X(N) / X(1).
Rearrange the USL into a straight line. For each N > 1, compute x = N − 1 and z = (N / C − 1) / (N − 1). If the USL holds, z = (α + β) + βx.
Fit a straight line through the three points by least squares. The slope is β and the intercept is α + β.
Predict the peak and check the fit at worker counts you didn't use. The fit says 13.57 million payments a second at 48 workers; the demo measured 13.56 million.
steps.code: peak = sqrt((1 - alpha) / beta) = sqrt(0.97055 / 0.000473) ≈ 45 workers fun usl(n: Int, alpha: Double, beta: Double) = n / (1.0 + alpha * (n - 1) + beta * n * (n - 1.0)) 975_610 * usl(48, 0.02945, 0.000473) // ≈ 13.57 million/s

lab.title: Fit the scaling curve, then find the COST
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 7 fail with NotImplementedError.

Read Settlement.kt. It is finished: the settlement batch on one thread and on a simulated shared-nothing cluster, with every step's cost added to a virtual clock. The totals are real, so the tests can check that both give the same answer.
In Scaling.kt, write amdahl, usl and uslPeak. They are one line each; the KDoc has the formulas.

Write fitUsl: turn each measurement into a point (N − 1, (N / C − 1) / (N − 1)), fit a straight line by least squares, and read β from the slope and α from intercept minus slope. One test feeds it exact USL data and expects α and β back to nine decimal places; another feeds it the measured batch and checks the predicted peak.
Write cost, then run the tests until all 7 pass. The last test finds the cluster's COST (16 workers) and shows that a slower shuffle makes it unbounded.
hints: Use toDouble() before you divide: n / c with an Int n is fine in Kotlin only because c is a Double, but (n - 1) on its own is an Int.
Least squares for a line: slope = Σ(x − x̄)(z − z̄) / Σ(x − x̄)², intercept = z̄ − slope × x̄. You don't need a library.
uslPeak must return Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY when β is zero or negative: without coherency cost the curve never turns down.
cost is (1..maxWorkers).firstOrNull { clusterSeconds(it) < singleThreadSeconds }. Note the strict <: equal time doesn't outperform.

drill.title: Fit the USL from memory
drill.prompt: Write fitUsl(measured: Map<Int, Double>): UslFit without looking: from throughput by worker count (including N = 1), return α, β and the single-worker throughput. Write down the straight line you fit before you write the code.

answer.html: // z = (N / C - 1) / (N - 1) = (alpha + beta) + beta * (N - 1) fun fitUsl(measured: Map<Int, Double>): UslFit { val single = measured.getValue(1) val points = measured.filterKeys { it > 1 }.map { (n, x) -> val c = x / single (n - 1.0) to (n / c - 1.0) / (n - 1.0) } val mx = points.map { it.first }.average() val mz = points.map { it.second }.average() val slope = points.sumOf { (x, z) -> (x - mx) * (z - mz) } / points.sumOf { (x, _) -> (x - mx) * (x - mx) } val intercept = mz - slope * mx return UslFit(alpha = intercept - slope, beta = slope, single = single) }

recap: Scaling up buys one bigger shared-memory machine (today up to 1,920 vCPUs and 32 TiB). It stops paying when price grows faster than size and the serial share caps the speed-up (Amdahl).
The USL, C(N) = N / (1 + α(N − 1) + βN(N − 1)), adds the cost of every pair of workers keeping in step; throughput peaks at √((1 − α) / β) and then falls.
Shared memory shares RAM, shared disk shares storage behind a lock manager (Oracle RAC), shared nothing shares only the network and must partition the data.

Cloud-native systems separate storage from compute: Aurora ships only redo records to six copies in three zones (write 4, read 3), Snowflake and Neon keep the durable copy in object storage. Always ask where the durable copy is and what is only a cache.
Serverless sells elasticity at the price of limits and cold starts; microservices sell team independence at the price of operations and cross-service consistency.
COST is the hardware a system needs to beat one good thread. Many published systems needed hundreds of cores or never got there, so measure it before you distribute.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to move the nightly settlement job from one big server to a 64-node cluster "so it scales". Explain what you'd measure first and why more nodes could make it slower.
explain.answer: First I'd measure how long one well-written thread takes, because a cluster has to beat that before it's worth anything. That's its COST, and published systems often needed hundreds of cores to beat one thread, mostly because of per-record framework overhead. Then I'd measure throughput at a few cluster sizes and fit the Universal Scalability Law. α is the serial part, like job startup and the final commit, which caps the speed-up the way Amdahl's law says. β is the cost of the nodes keeping in step, like a shuffle in which every node talks to every other; it grows with the number of pairs, so past the peak, √((1 − α) / β), each extra node makes the job slower. If one big server or a better algorithm meets the deadline, that's simpler to run and has fewer ways to fail.

deeper.html:
Where the USL comes from. Neil Gunther introduced the model in the early 1990s for transaction systems on parallel machines and later called it the Universal Scalability Law. It is empirical: it doesn't say why a system has a given α or β, only that most measured curves fit the shape. That's also its use. A fitted β well above zero is a signal to go looking for the thing every worker touches. And the fit can extrapolate the peak from measurements taken at small sizes, before you buy the big cluster.

Snowflake's reasons for leaving shared nothing. The 2016 Snowflake paper names three problems with tying data to the nodes that compute on it, in the cloud. Different workloads want different hardware: a bulk load wants I/O, a complex query wants CPU. Changing the cluster's size means moving data on the same nodes that are busy answering queries. And online upgrades get harder when every node holds unique data. Its answer was shared storage (S3) with many independent compute clusters, each caching what it reads, and assigning files to workers with consistent hashing so that resizing a warehouse doesn't move any data.

Aurora's numbers in perspective. The 35 times more transactions came from a write-only benchmark against MySQL mirrored synchronously across zones on EBS, the setup that suffers most from shipping pages. Aurora still writes six copies of every log record. It sends far less data per write, sends the six writes in parallel, and needs only the fastest four to answer, so one slow storage node, a gray failure in lesson 3's terms, doesn't slow commits down.

Cross-zone traffic as an architecture force. KIP-1150 quotes $0.02 per GiB for cross-zone traffic on AWS and $0.01 on Google Cloud, and nothing on Azure. A Kafka topic with three replicas in three zones sends every produced byte across zones twice for replication, and often again to consumers in other zones. At a few hundred MB/s that adds up to a larger bill than the brokers themselves, which is why "diskless" designs, which let object storage do the replication, appeared first as commercial products and then as a Kafka proposal.
